title: Almost 20 years of software development meets AI-assisted game development – Sudoku Shift
author: haf68k
selftext:
I've been working as a software developer for almost 20 years and wanted to spend more time building my own products.

For Game Off 2026, I created Sudoku Shift, a new take on classic Sudoku featuring a shift mechanic and real-time multiplayer.

I used AI tools to assist with coding, graphics, and audio.

The project combines traditional software engineering, game development, automated testing, and AI-assisted workflows.

The game is playable for free:

[https://hapheus.itch.io/sudoku-shift](https://hapheus.itch.io/sudoku-shift)

Source code:

[https://github.com/hapheus/sudoku-shift](https://github.com/hapheus/sudoku-shift)

I'm particularly interested in how other experienced developers integrate AI into their game development workflows.

comments.author: K_kkomi
comments.body:
This is really interesting! I've also been experimenting with AI-assisted game development, especially using tools like Claude Code.

One thing I've noticed is that AI can speed up implementation quite a bit, but designing good gameplay mechanics and making sure everything actually feels fun still takes a lot of human iteration.

I'm curious, how much of Sudoku Shift was built with AI compared to your own code and design decisions?

replies.author: haf68k
replies.body:
Absolutely! AI takes a lot of work off your hands, especially when it comes to implementation. But coming up with interesting gameplay mechanics and creative ideas still requires human input.

You need to know what you want and communicate it clearly. That's also one of the reasons I chose Sudoku as a foundation — the core rules are already well-defined. The same applies to the Easter eggs I included. You still need to come up with the ideas, define how they should work, and think about how players might discover them.

But to answer your question directly: I let AI handle the entire implementation of Sudoku Shift.

As a developer with around 20 years of experience, it was surprisingly difficult to resist the temptation to write code myself. And yes, I burned through quite a lot of tokens along the way. 😄

Was that necessary? No.  
Could I have achieved the same result faster and with fewer tokens by writing some of the code myself? Probably.  
So why did I do it anyway? Simply to learn.

AI-assisted development is still a relatively new discipline. In a way, we're all junior developers again, regardless of how many years of traditional software development experience we have.

Today's AI models are already capable of handling complete development tasks. But learning how to guide them, provide the right context, define clear requirements, and ensure quality is a skill of its own.

For me, Sudoku Shift wasn't just about building a game. It was also an experiment in learning how to develop software in a fundamentally different way.

And that's what made this project particularly interesting to me.

replies.author: K_kkomi
replies.body:
That's a really interesting experiment, especially coming from someone with 20 years of development experience. I think resisting the urge to jump in and write the code yourself must have been one of the hardest parts!

I'm also using Claude Code to build my own games, and I've noticed that clearly defining mechanics and explaining exactly what I want often takes more effort than I initially expected.

I guess the real skill is shifting from writing the code to knowing what to build and how to guide AI toward the right result. Thanks for sharing your experience!
